subject: Communication
title: How Politicians Persuade
description: A short lesson to help you apply How Politicians Persuade.

hook.text: A politician says 'I feel your pain' and poll numbers rise. Policy details barely move the needle.

buildup.text: Political persuasion relies heavily on identity, emotion, and tribal affiliation — not rational argument.

discovery.text: George Lakoff showed that political language uses metaphorical frames: 'tax relief' implies taxes are a burden.

twist.text: Voters rarely change their minds from arguments. They align with candidates who mirror their values.

climax.text: The most persuasive political tool isn't a fact sheet. It's a compelling personal story that says 'I'm like you.'

punchline.text: People don't vote for policies. They vote for mirrors.

quiz.question: What does George Lakoff's research show about political language?
options: Metaphorical frames shape how we think about issues

details.summary: Political persuasion combines rhetorical techniques, emotional appeals, tribal identity, and media strategy. Politicians use framing, repetition, enemy construction, and mythmaking to build coalitions. The emotional brain, not the rational brain, determines most political preferences.
details.whyItMatters: Democracy depends on informed voters. Understanding political persuasion techniques helps citizens evaluate candidates on policy rather than performance.
takeaways: Political persuasion targets emotions over rationality
Framing and repetition shape public perception of issues
Enemy construction unites supporters through shared opposition

faq.question: Why does repetition work so well in politics?
faq.answer: The illusory truth effect means repeated statements feel more true regardless of accuracy. Politicians repeat slogans and talking points knowing that familiarity breeds acceptance. Media coverage of repeated claims amplifies this effect even when the coverage is critical.

faq.question: How do politicians use tribal identity?
faq.answer: By framing issues as us versus them, politicians activate tribal loyalty that overrides policy evaluation. Voters support their team's positions even when those positions change. Group identity is processed in brain regions associated with personal identity and survival.
